Date: 2026-11-23
Start: 09:45 PT
Duration: ~57 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Briggs (NovaHealth CTO), Maya Lopez (NovaHealth ML Lead), Sanjay Patel (NovaHealth Infra)
Notes: demo + console walkthrough focused on quantization profiles, fallback rules, and operational controls
summary: High-level walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console: profiling INT8 and FP8 precision profiles, demonstrating latency vs quality tradeoffs, and explaining fallback/runbook strategies. Customer is evaluating for a pilot to reduce inference cost for clinical summarization. Key asks: runbench on customer prompts, confirm latency SLOs, produce security docs and Dedicated pricing.
topics:
1) Optimize console profiling flow
2) INT8 vs FP8 accuracy/loss examples
3) Throughput/latency impact and p50/p95 numbers
4) Fallback rules: auto-fallback to safer variant on quality regressions
5) KV/prefix caching and batching impacts
6) Dedicated vs Hosted considerations and security requirements
7) Next steps and pilot timeline
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Reed: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanna respect the hour here, quick intros. I'm Alex from Redwood, and Priya is our systems engineer.
[00:22] Tom Briggs: Hey Alex, Maya, Sanjay here from NovaHealth. We're excited — want to see how quant profiles can shave costs without wrecking the clinical summaries.
[00:34] Priya Nair: Great. We'll start in the Optimize console, run a quick profile then show an INT8 and FP8 compare. Note: some of the numbers we demo are from a sandbox so you might see a small delta vs your infra.
[00:48] Maya Lopez: Quick context, our main constraints: 1) p95 latency target is 450ms for the summarization endpoint, 2) we need fidelity for PHI redaction and clinical facts, 3) SOC2 and on-prem considerations for patient data.
[01:10] Alex Reed: Perfect, that maps to what we typically see. We'll show both latency-sensitive and quality-sensitive profiles and the fallback runbook you can use.
[01:25] Priya Nair: Opening the console now — Optimize > Precision Profiles. You can see agent-created qprofiles and an experimental FP8 candidate we ran. I'm going to trigger a sampling job on a short set so we can compare outputs inline.
[01:48] Maya Lopez: when you say FP8 candidate, is that a proprietary Redwood format or an open quant format?
[01:56] Priya Nair: It's a mixed-precision flow, implementation depends on the model. For Llama-style checkpoints we use our FP8 kernels, and for others we fall back to INT8 safe-modes. There's some nuance, so we'll show the quality diffs. Also note kernel selection and compilation matter a lot.
[02:18] Tom Briggs: And how do you handle KV cache / streaming? We need to keep latency low on short-turn prompts.
[02:26] Priya Nair: We keep prefix KV caching and streaming enabled for those routes; caching can cut p50 by ~20% for repeated prefixes. Important to tune prefix window and cache TTL.
[02:39] Alex Reed: We'll paste a link to the sandbox runbook and the precision playbook after the call (link in chat).
[02:48] Priya Nair: Alright starting the sample run — we'll show the three outputs: FP32 baseline, INT8 profile, FP8 profile. Give me a sec to load the test set.
[03:10] [00:03:10] (background typing)
[03:24] Priya Nair: Okay, results streaming in — first look at p50/p95: baseline FP32 p50 210ms p95 420ms; INT8 p50 150ms p95 350ms; FP8 p50 130ms p95 340ms on this GPU-backed sandbox. These are rough.
[03:52] Maya Lopez: Those p95 improvements are promising. But can you show an example where INT8 causes hallucination or degrades clinical accuracy?
[04:05] Priya Nair: Yep — here's a side-by-side output for the patient summary prompt. FP32: includes correct med list and no PHI leakage. INT8 example: small token substitution on medication dosage phrasing — not a hallucination per se but a fidelity artifact. FP8 output was closer to FP32 in wording but occasionally trimmed an explanatory clause.
[04:35] Tom Briggs: If INT8 changes a dosage wording that's a no-go for us. How do we gate that?
[04:42] Alex Reed: That's why we recommend a two-step strategy: sample-driven sensitivity analysis in Optimize, then apply a canary rollout with automatic rollback if quality metrics drop below threshold.
[04:54] Priya Nair: In the console you can create a safety test set — we call it a guardrail eval — and define rules, e.g., F1 score on medication extraction must be >0.95. If the profile fails, the routing layer falls back to a safer model variant or to Dedicated capacity with higher fidelity.
[05:22] Sanjay Patel: On fallback, is that per-request or per-route? We have mixed traffic — some low-risk and some high-risk endpoints.
[05:31] Priya Nair: Per-route policies are standard; you can also do per-customer tag routing. For high-risk endpoints you pin to FP32 or FP8 profile and block INT8. For mixed workloads we do adaptive routing with a small percentage to INT8 to measure.
[05:51] Maya Lopez: Can that be automated? We don't want manual toggles.
[05:55] Priya Nair: Yes, you can set automated canary thresholds with rollback triggers (quality drop or latency exceed). The console shows a graph and you can attach webhooks to your monitoring.
[06:10] Alex Reed: I'll note that for your pilot we often recommend starting with a 5-10% traffic experiment to validate metrics.
[06:19] Tom Briggs: For Dedicated deployment, do you support our KMS and HSM for key management? We have strict encryption policies.
[06:27] Alex Reed: Yes, Private Dedicated supports customer KMS/HSM integrations and brings control plane into your VPC. We'll include the KMS integration notes in the security pack.
[06:40] Sanjay Patel: Also SSO and audit logs — we need RBAC and long retention of audit trails.
[06:45] Alex Reed: SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, and extended audit retention are all available on enterprise plans; we'll attach the compliance matrix.
[06:55] Priya Nair: Back to the bench — here's a concrete token-level delta example. INT8 replaced a numeric token sequence with a near-synonym making a dosage ambiguous. The console flags that as a structural change and shows a delta heatmap.
[07:18] Maya Lopez: That heatmap looks useful. Are the diffs deterministic? We saw variance across runs.
[07:25] Priya Nair: There's some run-to-run noise, especially on FP8 with different kernel autotuning. We recommend running multiple seeds and using median metrics, and also sampling outputs to human review.
[07:38] Tom Briggs: How much dev effort to integrate the runbook and routing? Our platform is microservices behind an API gateway.
[07:47] Alex Reed: Integration is straightforward: you call the Redwood inference API the same way; routing, policies and fallback are configured in the console — we expose route tags and SDK hooks. If you need sidecar-style on-prem orchestration we have a package for that too.
[08:03] Sanjay Patel: Do you support per-token streaming and partial outputs because we stream to our UI?
[08:09] Priya Nair: Yes, streaming is supported. Note that with aggressive batching you trade off latency for throughput; streaming opens the door for early partial responses.
[08:24] Maya Lopez: Can we quantify cost delta? Rough per-token or per-request?
[08:30] Alex Reed: In our sandbox, INT8 reduced token compute cost by ~40% vs FP32; FP8 was ~50% on the right kernel/hardware, but your actual savings depend on sequence lengths and cache hit rates. We'll run a sample-based cost estimate as part of the pilot.
[08:54] Priya Nair: Also if you enable prefix/KV caching on repeated workflows the effective per-request cost drops further — we can show an add-on chart.
[09:05] Tom Briggs: For our regulatory team we'll need a reproducible benchmark and the exact kernel versions used. Can Redwood produce that?
[09:12] Alex Reed: Yes, the Optimize run export includes kernel tags, compilation flags, and model hashes. We'll include that in the bench artifact.
[09:24] [00:09:24] (link pasted in chat: https://redwood.com/sandbox/precision-playbook.pdf)
[09:40] Maya Lopez: On the quality metrics — you mentioned F1 for med extraction. Do you support custom metrics like clinical-accuracy or entity-level exact match?
[09:49] Priya Nair: Absolutely — you can register custom metrics in Optimize and we compute them across sampled outputs. The guardrail framework can use any registered metric for rollback triggers.
[10:03] Tom Briggs: Are there limitations on model types? Some of our workflows use a proprietary decoder architecture.
[10:10] Priya Nair: We support a wide range but proprietary models sometimes need a custom ingestion step. We'll try with your checkpoint in the pilot; early compatibility checks usually take 2-3 days.
[10:23] Alex Reed: For the pilot, timeline we propose: week 0 — share dataset and access details; week 1 — Redwood runs bench and shares initial report; week 2 — you validate and we set canary; week 3 — expand traffic or tune.
[10:39] Tom Briggs: That sounds reasonable. Are there any known worst-case failure modes we should plan for?
[10:44] Priya Nair: Worst-case we saw are silent degradation where a subtle factual error slips through. That's why we pair automated metrics with a human-in-the-loop sampling and the automatic fallback to safe variant.
[10:58] Maya Lopez: For human review, do you support webhooking outputs to our annotation platform?
[11:04] Priya Nair: Yes, we support webhooks and direct S3 exports for sampling.
[11:12] Sanjay Patel: Cost predictability is important — how do we avoid surprise charges during pilot spikes?
[11:19] Alex Reed: For Dedicated pilots we do committed capacity or caps. For hosted we can set rate limits and quota alerts; we'll propose a billing cap for the pilot.
[11:32] Tom Briggs: On the topic of fallback again, can we have conditional fallbacks: e.g., if metric X fails but latency is still under SLO, go to FP8; if both fail then route to FP32?
[11:44] Priya Nair: Yes — the policy engine supports multi-conditional rules. You can define priority levels and fallthrough variants.
[11:55] Alex Reed: I'll demonstrate a quick policy builder: create rule — metric threshold — select fallback model — set rollout % — save.
[12:08] [00:12:08] (screen share: policy builder demo)
[12:28] Priya Nair: For NovaHealth we might recommend primary: INT8 for low-risk, fallback to FP8 on quality drop, fallback to FP32 on repeated failures. This gives the most cost upside while preserving safety.
[12:46] Maya Lopez: How do we instrument our own telemetry into that decision? We want our APM to see when a request falls back.
[12:53] Priya Nair: We emit structured traces and events; you can attach tags that show in your APM and the console. There's also a webhook stream for fallback events.
[13:07] Tom Briggs: Are you able to show an example where you automatically rolled back in production?
[13:13] Priya Nair: Yes — quick story: a customer had a spike in out-of-distribution prompts which nudged quality down; auto-rollback engaged and directed traffic away from INT8 and ops never received a customer complaint. We can share a sanitized runbook.
[13:30] Alex Reed: moving on — let's talk about sampling frequency and how many samples you need to trust metrics.
[13:37] Priya Nair: For critical clinical metrics we recommend 3,000+ samples to get stable F1 numbers; for coarse checks 500 can surface big regressions. Sample selection should include edge-case prompts.
[13:50] Maya Lopez: We'll compile those edge cases in the corpus.
[13:54] Tom Briggs: On the console UI, can we tag models as 'clinical-safe' so product teams don't accidentally route to INT8?
[14:00] Priya Nair: Yes tags and route policies can enforce that. Also role-based access prevents non-admins from changing policies.
[14:10] Sanjay Patel: Regarding network topology for private deployment — do you support air-gapped on-prem installs?
[14:16] Alex Reed: We have an on-prem package for highly regulated customers; it requires a short eng integration plan and we help with the install.
[14:27] Maya Lopez: any notes about observability for token-level differences? We want to see where model changed tokens.
[14:33] Priya Nair: The diff heatmap shows token-level deltas and highlights substitutions, deletions, insertions. You can export samples to S3 for deeper analysis.
[14:47] Tom Briggs: For our compliance folks, we need a reproducible bench artifact we can archive.
[14:53] Alex Reed: Bench artifacts include model hash, kernel versions, compile flags, sample corpus, and the exact console configuration. It's exportable as a tarball.
[15:06] Maya Lopez: Are there licensing issues with FP8 kernels? Some vendors restrict redistribution.
[15:12] Priya Nair: We keep kernel metadata and if a vendor license restricts redistribution we surface that in the artifact; typically the runtime runs kernels in your cluster and we don't redistribute vendor binaries unless agreed.
[15:27] Tom Briggs: One more practical: what's rollback latency? If we detect regression, how fast can traffic be rerouted?
[15:33] Priya Nair: Policy enforcement is near-real-time — typically under 2 seconds to switch variants for new requests. Existing in-flight requests continue on the old path.
[15:46] Alex Reed: Ok we have about 20 minutes left, want to spin a longer bench on the full sample set? Priya can queue a longer job and we'll share results in a day.
[15:59] Tom Briggs: Yes please. We'll also want the kernel tags in the export.
[16:06] Priya Nair: Kicking off the 5k sample job now. Expect a report in ~24 hours with per-metric breakdowns and examples of failing prompts.
[16:20] Maya Lopez: Good. One question about caching — does the caching layer respect PII rules? We don't want any raw PHI cached outside our control.
[16:29] Sanjay Patel: that's important.
[16:32] Priya Nair: For Private/Dedicated you control where the cache lives; in Hosted we can mask or not cache sensitive fields. We have built-in redaction and prefix filters.
[16:47] Tom Briggs: okay that helps.
[16:50] Alex Reed: Quick operational ask — what's your target go/no-go for pilot by date?
[16:57] Tom Briggs: We aim to decide by mid-December, budget cycle. So bench results by end of November fit well.
[17:06] Alex Reed: Good, aligns nicely. We'll follow up with the security pack and pilot docs.
[17:13] [00:17:13] (Priya pastes bench job link in chat)
[17:27] Maya Lopez: Regarding post-deploy monitoring, can we get daily drift reports?
[17:34] Priya Nair: Yes — drift alerts and periodic quality summaries are supported; you can configure cadence.
[17:44] Tom Briggs: Can Redwood integrate with our PagerDuty for critical fallback events?
[17:50] Alex Reed: Yes webhooks to PagerDuty are supported; we'll include a sample integration.
[17:59] Priya Nair: As we close the demo, quick recap of recommended pilot settings: 1) Run bench across FP32/INT8/FP8, 2) establish guardrail metrics and 3) start with 5-10% canary with auto-rollback.
[18:18] Tom Briggs: Sounds good. Any immediate blockers?
[18:21] Alex Reed: none from our side; we just need the sample corpus and access plan.
[18:27] Maya Lopez: I'll share the dataset link today.
[18:31] Sanjay Patel: I'll coordinate infra access and SSO details.
[18:35] Alex Reed: Great — we'll send the security pack and pricing later today.
[18:40] Priya Nair: One last note: if you have models with extremely long context windows the tradeoffs shift; we can provide a separate tuning session for long-context tuning.
[18:53] Tom Briggs: We'll flag that if it becomes relevant.
[18:57] Alex Reed: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff once bench results are in.
[19:05] Maya Lopez: Thanks all.
[19:08] Tom Briggs: Thanks, bye.
[19:11] (meeting ends)
